claims.text: High-entropy superconducting alloys designed through controlled compositional complexity and microstructure will exhibit enhanced superconducting properties compared with conventional superconductors.
High-entropy superconducting alloys will exhibit more robust superconducting properties than conventional superconductors.
The initial material is a polycrystalline high-entropy alloy that is normally conducting at room temperature.
Advanced synthesis and computational design can systematically vary the alloy composition and microstructure.
Systematic variation of composition and microstructure can tune electron–phonon coupling.
Superconductivity in the proposed alloy emerges under cryogenic conditions.
Controlled compositional complexity produces an optimized microstructure with reduced defect density.
The optimized microstructure fosters favorable electron–phonon interactions.
The multicomponent nature of the alloy enhances electron–phonon coupling.
The multicomponent alloy mitigates detrimental scattering and defect effects.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling enables a higher and more robust critical temperature.
The experimental alloy will have a higher superconducting critical temperature than conventional superconductors such as Nb3Sn.
The experimental alloy will maintain superconductivity under more robust operational conditions than Nb3Sn.
Nb3Sn has a lower critical temperature than the proposed high-entropy alloy.
Improvement depends on successful control of impurity levels and microstructural uniformity.
Processing deviations or compositional inhomogeneity may negate the anticipated superconducting benefits.
The relationship among composition, microstructure, and electron–phonon coupling strength has not been fully quantified.
